age6_8.summary: A scientist who found two new elements and won two Nobel Prizes.
age6_8.body:
Marie Curie was a scientist. She was born in Poland in 1867 [1].

When she was young, girls in Poland were not allowed to go to university. So she moved to France to study [1].

She found two brand new materials that nobody knew about. She named one polonium, after Poland [2].

She discovered that some materials give off invisible rays. She called this radioactivity [2].

She won the Nobel Prize twice. Almost nobody has ever done that [1].

In a war, she built X-ray vans and drove them to help wounded soldiers [1].

age9_12.summary: The physicist and chemist who discovered radium and polonium and won two Nobel Prizes.
age9_12.body:
Marie Curie was a Polish-French scientist who did the foundational work on radioactivity [1].

## Getting an education

She was born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw in 1867, when Poland was under Russian rule and women were barred from university there.

She worked as a governess for years, sending money to support her sister's studies in Paris, on the agreement that her sister would later support her. She finally reached Paris in 1891 and enrolled at the Sorbonne, studying in poverty [1].

## The discovery

Henri Becquerel had noticed that uranium gave off mysterious rays. Curie took up the question for her doctoral research.

She measured the rays precisely and found something crucial: the strength depended only on how much uranium was present, not on its chemical form. That meant the rays came from inside the atom itself — not from a chemical reaction [2].

This was a genuinely radical conclusion at a time when atoms were thought indivisible.

She also found that a uranium ore called pitchblende was more radioactive than pure uranium. Something else in it had to be even more active.

Working with her husband Pierre, and processing tonnes of ore by hand in a leaking shed, she isolated two new elements in 1898: polonium, named for her homeland, and radium [2].

## Two Nobel Prizes

In 1903 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre and Becquerel. She was initially left off the nomination, and was added after Pierre objected [1].

In 1911 she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone, for the discovery of polonium and radium.

She remains the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences [1].

## The war

When the First World War began, Curie realised X-rays could locate shrapnel and broken bones in wounded soldiers.

She developed mobile X-ray units, raised the money, learned to drive, and took them to the front. They are estimated to have helped over a million wounded men [1].

## The cost

The dangers of radiation were not understood at the time. Curie carried radioactive samples in her pockets and worked without protection.

She died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, a blood disorder most likely caused by her long exposure. Her notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes [1].

teen.summary: Polish-French physicist and chemist whose work established radioactivity as an atomic property, and the only laureate honoured in two distinct sciences.
teen.body:
Marie Curie (1867-1934) was a physicist and chemist whose investigations of radioactivity reshaped the understanding of the atom [1].

## Background

Born Maria Skłodowska in Russian-partitioned Warsaw, she was excluded from higher education on grounds of both nationality and sex. She attended the clandestine "Flying University" and worked as a governess for several years under an arrangement to fund her sister's Paris studies before her own.

She entered the Sorbonne in 1891, completing degrees in physics and mathematics in conditions of considerable hardship [1].

## The central insight

Following Becquerel's observation of uranium emissions, Curie undertook systematic quantitative measurement using an electrometer developed by Pierre Curie and his brother.

Her decisive finding was that emission intensity depended solely on the quantity of uranium present, and was unaffected by chemical combination, temperature or physical state.

The implication was radical: the phenomenon was a property of the atom itself, not of molecular arrangement. At a time when the atom was held to be indivisible and immutable, this was a fundamental challenge, and it opened the path to understanding atomic structure [2].

She further observed that pitchblende exhibited greater activity than its uranium content could account for, implying an undiscovered and more active constituent.

## Isolation of polonium and radium

Working with Pierre Curie in a converted shed, Curie processed tonnes of pitchblende residue through repeated chemical separation, tracking fractions by measured activity rather than by chemical expectation.

Both polonium and radium were announced in 1898. Isolating a decigram of radium chloride required years of physically punishing labour [2].

The Curies declined to patent their radium isolation process, holding that scientific findings should remain freely available — a decision that left them without income from a substance that became commercially valuable.

## Recognition

The 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics was shared with Pierre Curie and Becquerel. The original nomination omitted Marie Curie; her inclusion followed Pierre's intervention with the nominating committee [1].

The 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to her alone for the discovery of polonium and radium. She remains the only individual to have received Nobel Prizes in two distinct scientific disciplines [1].

## Radiology in the First World War

Recognising the surgical value of radiographic localisation of shrapnel and fractures, Curie organised mobile radiological units. She secured funding and vehicles, obtained a driving licence, trained operators, and served at the front herself.

The programme is estimated to have served over a million wounded personnel [1].

## Radiation injury

The hazards of ionising radiation were unrecognised during the greater part of her career. Curie handled active sources without shielding and worked in contaminated conditions for decades.

She died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, attributed with high confidence but not absolute certainty to cumulative radiation exposure. Her laboratory notebooks remain significantly contaminated and are stored under shielding [1].

adult.summary: Polish-French physicist and chemist (1867-1934) whose quantitative work established radioactivity as an atomic rather than molecular phenomenon, and who isolated polonium and radium.
adult.body:
Marie Curie, born Maria Salomea Skłodowska, was a physicist and chemist whose research programme established radioactivity as an atomic property and contributed decisively to the dissolution of the indivisible atom [1].

## Formation

Born in Warsaw under Russian partition, she was excluded from formal higher education by both imperial policy and sex. She participated in the underground Flying University and worked as a governess under a reciprocal arrangement funding her sister's medical studies in Paris.

She matriculated at the Sorbonne in 1891, taking licences in physics and mathematics. She subsequently became the first woman appointed to a professorship at the University of Paris, succeeding Pierre Curie after his death in 1906 [1].

## The atomic character of radioactivity

Curie's doctoral research followed Becquerel's 1896 observation of penetrating emissions from uranium salts. Her methodological contribution was quantitative: employing the piezoelectric quartz electrometer developed by Pierre and Jacques Curie, she measured ionisation currents with precision unavailable to qualitative photographic methods.

The critical result was that activity was proportional to the mass of uranium present and independent of chemical combination, physical state or temperature.

The inference — that the emission originates within the atom and is not a chemical process — was profound. It contradicted the prevailing conception of the atom as stable and indivisible, and it identified radioactivity as a means of probing atomic structure. Rutherford and Soddy's subsequent theory of atomic transmutation proceeded from this foundation [2].

Curie also introduced the term *radioactivity*.

## Discovery of polonium and radium

Observing that pitchblende exhibited activity exceeding that attributable to its uranium content, Curie inferred an unidentified, more active component. The consequent programme inverted normal analytical practice: fractions were tracked by measured radioactivity rather than by anticipated chemical behaviour, making activity itself the analytical instrument.

Polonium and radium were both announced in 1898. Preparation of a decigram of radium chloride required processing on the order of tonnes of residue over four years under poor laboratory conditions [2].

The Curies declined to patent the isolation procedure. The decision was deliberate and reflected a principled position on scientific openness; its practical effect was to exclude them from revenue as radium acquired substantial commercial value.

## Honours and their circumstances

The 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded jointly to Becquerel and the Curies. The initial nomination submitted to the Academy named only Becquerel and Pierre Curie; Marie Curie's inclusion followed Pierre's representation to the committee. The episode is documented and is properly reported [1].

The 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was conferred on her alone. She remains the sole recipient of Nobel Prizes in two different scientific fields.

The 1911 award coincided with a French press campaign concerning her private life, in the course of which she was subjected to xenophobic and misogynistic attack; some parties suggested she decline the prize, and she travelled to Stockholm and accepted it.

## Wartime radiology

During the First World War Curie established mobile radiological units — *petites Curies* — to provide forward radiographic capability for surgical localisation of projectiles and fractures. She raised finance, procured and equipped vehicles, obtained a driving licence, trained approximately 150 operators, and served in the field with her daughter Irène.

The service is estimated to have benefited more than a million wounded personnel, and constitutes one of the earliest large-scale deployments of diagnostic imaging in military medicine [1].

## Radiation injury and legacy

The stochastic and cumulative effects of ionising radiation were not understood during most of Curie's working life. She handled unshielded sources routinely and worked in persistently contaminated environments.

Death in 1934 was from aplastic anaemia. Attribution to occupational radiation exposure is an interpretation supported by strong circumstantial evidence rather than a directly demonstrated causal finding, and should be stated as such. Her notebooks and effects remain contaminated and are held under shielded conditions [1].

Her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1935 for the discovery of artificial radioactivity.
